newsitem.title: ITALY: Albanian wreck casts shadow over Italian-led force.
newsitem.headline: Albanian wreck casts shadow over Italian-led force.

text.p: Italy searched for more victims of an Albanian shipwreck on Monday as politicians, worried about the reception of an imminent Italian-led mission to the impoverished state, argued over the tragedy.
Grieving survivors, who lost husbands, wives and young children in Albania's worst maritime disaster since World War Two, demanded action from Rome.
"We want the truth," one man told RAI television in the southern port of Brindisi where a magistrate investigating Friday's sinking questioned some survivors.
The navy, which has rejected accusations that it was to blame, said an aircraft was flying over a 30 mile area searching for survivors, while the patrolling frigate Zeffiro was on the scene.
The small Albanian harbour patrol vessel crowded with refugees from the southern port of Vlore capsized and sank after colliding with a navy ship trying to turn it away.
Four bodies were recovered on Friday and 34 people rescued.
Pandeli Pasko, the Albanian ambassador to Italy, told Italy's Channel 5 television he had compiled an updated list of people presumed dead and the total was 83.

A statement from the Italian Senate said the upper house of parliament's defence and foreign affairs committees would meet on Tuesday to discuss the tragedy that has cast a cloud over the planned force for Albania.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta were expected to speak.

Italian ships have been ordered by Rome to intercept Albanian boats heading for Italy and force them to turn back. Some 13,000 people have flooded into Italy in recent weeks and Italy maintains most have fled for economic reasons.
The navy denies it is carrying out a formal blockade, saying patrols are engaged in dissuasive action.

Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi, who interrupted his Easter vacation in Sardinia to fly to Brindisi on his private jet, called on Sunday for the tactics to end and said he had not been fully informed by Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
"This blockade (must) be suspended absolutely because it is hard to see where it is leading us to," Berlusconi, who seemed overcome by emotion during the visit, told reporters.
The former prime minister said the tragedy had complicated the country's close ties with Albania.
"It will certainly make our mission in Albania more difficult because many Albanians will undoubtedly have negative feelings against us," Berlusconi told reporters.

The multinational force is due to secure Vlore, the northern port of Durres and Tirana airport for supplies, running short after the unrest. Albania's crisis was sparked by protests at the failure of savings schemes since late 1996.
Junior Foreign Minister Piero Fassino countered Berlusconi and said politicians must not exploit the tragedy.

"It is truly alarming that Berlusconi should go and cry in Brindisi when a large number of Forza Italia members have in recent days constantly accused the government of being too benevolent and permissive," he countered.

"And it is even more alarming that a section of the political class should abandon themselves to this sort of exploitation at a time when thousands of our boys are leaving for Albania on a humanitarian mission of peace.

"This all risks creating a hostile climate around our men," Fassino said. "What happened in the Straits of Otranto cannot hide the fact that Italy has given shelter in a civilised fashion to almost 13,000 Albanians in just a few days."
Italy has said it wants the Albania mission to start as soon as possible but has yet to fix a precise date.
About 7,000 people protested in Vlore on Sunday with some demonstrators warning the Italians to stay away.
